Adform detected the incident on July 27, 2026, removed the malicious code, notified affected clients, and reported it to authorities. Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js then beaconed to C2 · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Poison Adform Script to Swap Crypto Wallet Addresses Across Customer Sit
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Adform crypto-stealer C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Adform crypto-stealer C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker C2/exfil host used by the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js supply-chain payload. The beacon fires on page load and carries the visitor's page hostname and path, so any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that rendered the trojanized script. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the single atomic C2/exfil IOC confirmed by BleepingComputer, Beaumont (DoublePulsar) and it-connect; the IP is attacker-owned with no legitimate use, so any egress to it is a confirmed compromised-browser signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firms-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat intel analyst or malware sandbox on the corporate network intentionally connecting to the IOC to validate it
  • IR team detonating the captured script in a lab that shares the corporate egress IP
  • The VPS IP later being re-assigned to a benign service (weeks after takedown), causing stale-IOC hits
  • A vulnerability scanner or IOC-sweep tool probing the address
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-lab-vm")  // exclude known detonation hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect msedge.exe/chrome.exe/firefox.exe) and the user; pull the RemoteUrl/referrer to learn which downstream site served the poisoned Adform script. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at the egress firewall/proxy, force-clear the affected browser cache on the host (the trojaned trackpoint-async.js persists in cache after Adform's fix), and warn the user any crypto address copied that session may be swapped. 3) Hunt: pivot on all internal hosts that reached this IP in the last 14 days, and check for any crypto transactions initiated from those users around the beacon time for redirected payments.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js then beaconed to C2 AIDelivery Medium
Correlates web-proxy retrieval of s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js with a subsequent connection to the attacker C2 84.32.102.230, scoping exactly which endpoints rendered the trojanized supply-chain script. The C2 correlation removes the huge false-positive volume of legitimate Adform ad traffic. Rationale: Uses the confirmed delivery path s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js and gates it on the confirmed C2 IP 84.32.102.230, so only endpoints that both loaded the poisoned resource and beaconed are surfaced — precise supply-chain exposure scoping without alerting on benign post-fix Adform loads. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firms-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A shared NAT/egress IP causing a benign host's Adform load to falsely correlate with an unrelated host's C2 hit behind the same SourceIP (proxy environments)
  • Legitimate Adform ad traffic on a host that independently triggered the C2 IOC via a sandbox test
  • Cached/replayed benign trackpoint-async.js load after Adform's remediation on a host also flagged for stale-IOC C2 hit
  • Ad QA/marketing team intentionally loading Adform test tags on a lab host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the same host (not just same egress IP) both retrieved trackpoint-async.js and reached 84.32.102.230; identify the user and the downstream site (referrer) that carried the poisoned tag. 2) Contain: force browser cache clear on the endpoint to purge the trojaned script, block the C2 IP, and notify the user to re-verify any crypto wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: enumerate every internal site/property embedding Adform tags, and expand the proxy search to all hosts that fetched trackpoint-async.js between 20-27 July to build the full exposed-user list for cache-clear advisories.

DeviceNetworkEvents

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

status: experimental

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'

Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 17 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A fake browser update served over hijacked hotel Wi-Fi has been used to deliver CornFlake, a remote access trojan (RAT) that can capture webcam images, microphone audio, and keystrokes, Microsoft said in its latest report. Researchers track the operation as CaptiveCrunch and attribute it to Storm-2945. It assesses Storm-2945 to be an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, also known as

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch DNS hijack: resolution of Microsoft-impersonating captive-portal domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch ClickFix: shell launched with attacker-supplied command referencing campaign domains · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake persistence: 'Cloud Sync Service' / svchost32 service, Run key and scheduled task · [LLM] CornFlake masquerade: svchost32.exe executing from %APPDATA%\svchost32\ · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CornFlake C2: svchost32 implant beaconing to CaptiveCrunch IOC infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CornFlake surveillance: implant loading webcam/audio/screen-capture libraries · [LLM] ChocoShell token theft: access to .tbres Token Broker / WAM cache files · [LLM] CaptiveCrunch Entra token replay: sign-ins from Storm-2945 IP infrastructure · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
CaptiveCrunch DNS hijack: resolution of Microsoft-impersonating captive-portal domains AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint contact with the Storm-2945 Microsoft-spoofing landing/device-code domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com) served over hijacked hotel captive-portal DNS. Because the gateway forges DNS to redirect connectivity checks, any device resolving these look-alike domains is being redirected to attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the five confirmed pre-extracted domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com) plus the four attacker IPs — these are hard IOCs, not behavioural heuristics, so resolution equals redirection to Storm-2945 infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst detonating IOCs in a sandbox on a managed host
  • Corporate proxy/DNS sinkhole pre-resolving flagged domains for logging
  • Brand-protection / typosquat monitoring tooling that intentionally resolves look-alike domains
  • A legitimately-registered unrelated service later parking one of these domains after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device, the network it was on (compare public IP to known corporate egress vs. hotel/venue), and which process initiated the resolution. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force full-tunnel VPN, revoke Entra ID sessions/refresh tokens for the signed-in user, and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for svchost32.exe drops, service 'Cloud Sync Service', and beacons to the four IOC IPs; check Entra sign-in logs for device-code grants from the same timeframe.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity

CaptiveCrunch ClickFix: shell launched with attacker-supplied command referencing campaign domains AIExploitation High
Hunts the ClickFix execution step where victims are told to open a terminal/Run dialog and paste an attacker-supplied command. Fires when cmd/powershell/mshta/curl runs a command line containing the CaptiveCrunch delivery domains, indicating manual execution of the CornFlake/ChocoShell payload cradle. Rationale: Anchors on the article's ClickFix 'open a terminal and run an attacker-supplied command' behaviour, made high-fidelity by requiring one of the five confirmed campaign domains in the command line rather than a generic browser-spawns-shell heuristic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/004/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copy/pasting IOC domains into a terminal during investigation
  • Help-desk troubleshooting script that curls a health-check URL happening to share a substring
  • Security awareness phishing-simulation payloads referencing look-alike domains
  • Automated IOC-sweep scripts run by the SOC that echo the domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full command line — confirm it is a download/execute cradle (Invoke-Expression, curl -o, mshta http) targeting attacker infra, and identify the parent (explorer.exe = Run dialog paste, browser = link). 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process tree, revoke the user's Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for svchost32.exe under %APPDATA%\svchost32\, the 'Cloud Sync Service' service, .tbres access, and outbound to the four IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("deltaode.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("deltaode.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake persistence: 'Cloud Sync Service' / svchost32 service, Run key and scheduled task AIInstallation High
Hunts CornFlake's persistence footprint — a service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service', a Run key, and a scheduled task pointing at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe. Article-specific because it keys on the exact service/display name and drop path, not generic autostart. Rationale: Keys on the exact article artifacts: service name svchost32, display name 'Cloud Sync Service', and the %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe binary path — none of which collide with legitimate Windows svchost.exe under System32. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party app coincidentally naming a folder 'svchost32' (extremely rare)
  • EDR/backup software creating a service with 'Sync' in the display name
  • Admin restoring a system image that replays old service-install events
  • Internal red-team replaying CornFlake TTPs during an exercise
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the service binary resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (never legitimate) and note the writing process. 2) Contain: isolate host; stop and delete the svchost32 service, Run value, and scheduled task in one pass — CornFlake runs a watchdog, so remove all persistence artifacts and the binary together, then re-scan to confirm no re-creation. 3) Hunt: pivot to network events for svchost32.exe beacons to the IOC IPs and to .tbres/browser-cred access on the same host.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32")
   or (RegistryValueData has @"svchost32\svchost32.exe")
   or (RegistryKey has @"CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValueData has "svchost32")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName has "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has @"svchost32\svchost32.exe" or ServiceName has "Cloud Sync Service"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CornFlake Cloud Sync Service / svchost32 Persistence

CornFlake masquerade: svchost32.exe executing from %APPDATA%\svchost32\ AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of a process named svchost32.exe from outside System32 — specifically the CornFlake self-copy at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only runs from System32/SysWOW64 and is never named 'svchost32', making any such process high-fidelity. Rationale: The literal binary name 'svchost32.exe' and its %APPDATA%\svchost32\ path are unique CornFlake artifacts from the article; genuine svchost.exe is always System32/SysWOW64, so both name and location deviate. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/005/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A poorly-named legitimate utility that happens to ship 'svchost32.exe' (very rare)
  • Malware-analysis VM where an analyst renamed a sample to svchost32.exe
  • Portable app extracted to AppData that mimics service naming
  • Red-team infrastructure using the same masquerade name in an exercise
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" or FolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the SHA256 and full path; confirm it is not a signed Microsoft binary. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe along with its service/Run/task persistence (watchdog will otherwise re-drop). 3) Hunt: retro-hunt the SHA256 across the fleet and pivot to network beacons from this process to the four IOC IPs and deltaode.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
   or (FileName =~ "svchost.exe" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and FolderPath has @"\AppData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake surveillance: implant loading webcam/audio/screen-capture libraries AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CornFlake implant (svchost32.exe from AppData) loading multimedia capture DLLs used for webcam, microphone, and screenshot collection. This targets the surveillance-collection phase via image-load telemetry, a different pivot from process-create or network detections. Rationale: Scopes to the confirmed CornFlake implant path (%APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe) and requires ≥2 capture-related DLLs, matching the article's webcam/microphone/screenshot capabilities; Sentinel lacks a clean image-load table so that field is left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1125/
ATT&CKT1125 T1123 T1113
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate conferencing/recording apps loading the same media DLLs (excluded here by the svchost32 AppData path)
  • EDR emulation loading multimedia libraries during a scan
  • A renamed benign process at that exact path during analysis
  • Screen-recording utilities portable-installed under AppData
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading process is the AppData svchost32.exe implant and correlate with active webcam/mic device usage or screenshot files staged in %APPDATA%. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill process, and notify the affected user their device may have been under surveillance (rotate any credentials typed while compromised). 3) Hunt: look for outbound transfer of staged captures to the IOC IPs and for clipboard/keystroke collection artifacts on the same host.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
   and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| where FileName in~ ("avicap32.dll","mfcore.dll","mfplat.dll","mmdevapi.dll","audioses.dll","gdiplus.dll","dxgi.dll")
| summarize LoadedLibs = make_set(FileName), count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where array_length(LoadedLibs) >= 2
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
   and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| where FileName in~ ("avicap32.dll","mfcore.dll","mfplat.dll","mmdevapi.dll","audioses.dll","gdiplus.dll","dxgi.dll")
| summarize LoadedLibs = make_set(FileName), count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(LoadedLibs) >= 2
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 @Image:(*\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\svchost32.exe OR *\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\SVCHOST32.EXE) @ImageLoaded:(*avicap32.dll* OR *mfcore.dll* OR *mmdevapi.dll* OR *audioses.dll* OR *gdiplus.dll*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\AppData\\Roaming\\svchost32\\svchost32\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

ChocoShell token theft: access to .tbres Token Broker / WAM cache files AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ChocoShell's in-memory PowerShell theft of M365/Azure AD access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in the Token Broker cache. Fires on non-standard processes touching the Token Broker cache path or command lines referencing .tbres — enabling MFA-satisfied session replay. Rationale: Uses the article's specific ChocoShell tradecraft — reading .tbres files from the Token Broker cache to steal WAM/M365 refresh tokens — which is rarely touched by user-space PowerShell and never by CornFlake's svchost32. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1528 T1539 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Entra/Office troubleshooting scripts (e.g. clearing Token Broker cache) run by IT
  • Endpoint management agents enumerating the WAM cache
  • A developer inspecting .tbres files during auth debugging
  • Backup software indexing the LocalAppData tree including TokenBroker\Cache
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe") and ActorUsername !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process read/enumerated .tbres files and whether it was the AppData svchost32 implant or an interactive PowerShell. 2) Contain: revoke the user's Entra ID refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions), reset password, and enforce reauthentication; isolate host. 3) Hunt: correlate Entra non-interactive sign-ins from the IOC IPs (token replay), and check other hosts for the same .tbres access pattern.
let TokenActors = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","svchost32.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".tbres", @"TokenBroker\Cache", "TokenBroker")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine;
let FileTouches = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache" and FileName endswith ".tbres"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","svchost32.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName;
union TokenActors, FileTouches
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","svchost32.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".tbres", "TokenBroker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake C2: svchost32 implant beaconing to CaptiveCrunch IOC infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the CornFlake implant (svchost32.exe in AppData) or any host to the four confirmed Storm-2945 C2 IPs and deltaode.com. Combines the masquerading process identity with hard network IOCs for the remote-shell/beacon phase. Rationale: Four confirmed C2 IPs plus deltaode.com are hard IOCs; pairing them with InitiatingProcessFileName/folder surfaces which process (ideally svchost32.exe) is beaconing, satisfying the remote-shell C2 behaviour from the article. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1219 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox deliberately connecting to IOC IPs
  • Firewall/IDS test traffic validating IOC blocklists
  • IP re-assignment after takedown to a benign hosting tenant
  • Security scanner probing the IOC IPs from a corporate host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if svchost32.exe from AppData, treat as confirmed CornFlake C2. 2) Contain: block the four IPs and deltaode.com at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the process and remove persistence. 3) Hunt: retro-hunt all four IPs across firewall/proxy/EDR fleet-wide, and correlate with Entra token-replay sign-ins from the same infrastructure.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
   or RemoteUrl =~ "deltaode.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch Entra token replay: sign-ins from Storm-2945 IP infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts interactive and non-interactive Entra ID sign-ins originating from the four confirmed CaptiveCrunch C2 IPs — the signature of device-code-grant abuse and stolen WAM/refresh-token replay that yields MFA-satisfied access without a browser cookie. Rationale: The four IOC IPs are attacker infrastructure; any Entra sign-in from them (especially non-interactive) indicates stolen-token/device-code replay described in the article — a distinct identity-plane pivot from the endpoint detections. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/
ATT&CKT1621 T1550.001 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately on a hotel network whose egress IP overlaps a since-reassigned IOC IP
  • Security team validating IOC IPs against sign-in logs from a test account
  • Threat-intel enrichment service resolving these IPs
  • VPN/proxy exit node coincidentally sharing an IOC IP after takedown
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the account(s), whether the sign-in was non-interactive (token replay) and which resource/app was accessed. 2) Contain: revoke all refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions), reset credentials, block the IOC IPs via Conditional Access named locations, and disable the device-code flow where not needed. 3) Hunt: review the account's mailbox rules, OAuth grants, and downstream access for the session; correlate to the endpoint that ran CornFlake/ChocoShell.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive, ErrorCode, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(SigninLogs
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where IPAddress in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive="Interactive", ResultType),
(AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where IPAddress in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, ClientAppUsed, IsInteractive="NonInteractive", ResultType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any

references:

author: Clankerusecase

logsource:

detection:

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS prototype-pollution PATCH payload ($pullAll __proto__ publicApiProjection) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact CVE-2026-53609 exploitation request: an HTTP PATCH to an ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoint whose body carries the prototype-pollution key (`$pullAll` / `__proto__` / `publicApiProjection`). Requires a WAF or reverse proxy that logs request bodies. The literal token `__proto__.publicApiProjection` never appears in legitimate CMS traffic, making this near-zero-FP. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit strings: `$pullAll`, `__proto__`, and the gadget property `publicApiProjection` sent via PATCH to `/api/v1/@apostrophecms/`. These tokens have no legitimate use in CMS body traffic. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory DB and TheHackerWire write-up which confirm CVSS 9.1 and the identical mechanism. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Burp, Nuclei, Acunetix) running prototype-pollution test templates against the CMS
  • Internal pentest / red-team validating CVE-2026-53609
  • Developer testing the patch or reproducing the PoC in staging
  • A WAF replaying/echoing a blocked payload into a downstream log the SIEM also ingests (double-count)
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and RequestClientApplication !has "Burp" and SourceIP !in ("<scanner-vlan-not-applicable>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is external and the PATCH returned 200; pull the full request body to verify the `__proto__.publicApiProjection` key. Check whether a valid editor bearer token accompanied it (needed for exploitation). 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF, revoke/rotate the editor session/token that authorized the PATCH, and restart the Node.js process (the pollution persists in memory until restart). 3) Hunt: pivot to all subsequent unauthenticated GETs from any IP to `/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user` and `/global` returning 200 (see the auth-bypass UC); confirm patch to Apostrophe >= 4.31.0.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "@apostrophecms" or DestinationServiceName has "apostrophe"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__", "pullAll", "publicApiProjection")
      or Message has_any ("__proto__", "$pullAll", "publicApiProjection")
      or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__", "$pullAll", "publicApiProjection")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationServiceName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS unauthenticated authorization bypass — source flips from 401/403 to 200 on protected API AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the post-exploitation impact of CVE-2026-53609: after Object.prototype is polluted, unauthenticated requests to piece-type REST endpoints (/user, /global) that used to return notfound/401/403 now return 200. Alerts when a source IP transitions from denied to allowed on these endpoints, indicating the process-wide auth gate has been bypassed. Rationale: Targets the article's confirmed bypass behaviour: `/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user` returns a paginated 200 with no credentials where it previously returned `notfound`. The denied->allowed transition per source IP is the temporal fingerprint of the process-wide gate collapsing. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming unauthenticated access to /user and /global endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An operator legitimately enabled `publicApiProjection` config on a piece-type, making /api responses public by design
  • A NAT/proxy egress IP shared by both anonymous visitors and authenticated editors, blurring the denied->allowed picture
  • CDN or health-check IP that previously 404'd a path then hit a valid one
  • Deployment that changed the API's auth requirements (feature flag / config push) around the same window
Suppression filter
| where SampleOkUri !has "publicApiProjection"  // exclude endpoints intentionally made public via config
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the flagged CIp, confirm the 200 responses carried NO Authorization bearer token and returned real record data. Correlate with any PATCH containing `$pullAll`/`__proto__` from any source in the preceding window. 2) Contain: restart the Node.js process to clear the in-memory prototype pollution; block offending IPs; take the instance out of the load balancer if data was exposed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every piece-type endpoint (not just /user, /global) that returned 200 unauthenticated; assess what records were read for data-exposure/breach notification; patch to Apostrophe >= 4.31.0.
let lookback = 3d;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where CsMethod == "GET"
| summarize DeniedCount = countif(ScStatus in (401, 403, 404)),
            FirstDenied = minif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus in (401, 403, 404)),
            OkCount = countif(ScStatus == 200),
            FirstOk = minif(TimeGenerated, ScStatus == 200),
            SampleOkUri = anyif(CsUriStem, ScStatus == 200)
          by CIp
| where DeniedCount > 0 and OkCount > 0 and FirstOk > FirstDenied   // 401/403/404 history, then flipped to 200
| project CIp, DeniedCount, FirstDenied, OkCount, FirstOk, SampleOkUri
| order by FirstOk desc

ApostropheCMS exploit chain — pollution PATCH followed by unauthenticated 200 from same source AIExploitation High
Correlates the two halves of CVE-2026-53609 into one high-confidence signal: a PATCH to an ApostropheCMS piece-type endpoint (the pollution vector) followed within a short window by a successful unauthenticated GET to a protected endpoint (/user or /global) from the same source IP. The temporal chain removes the ambiguity of either event alone. Rationale: Combines the article's two observable stages — the `$pullAll` PATCH and the subsequently-successful unauthenticated GET to /user or /global — keyed on a shared source IP within 60s. This is the most specific expression of the documented attack sequence and the lowest-FP of the web detections. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated web scanner that PATCHes then immediately re-GETs endpoints as part of a crawl
  • Editor legitimately PATCHing a doc then loading a public-projection-enabled listing from the same egress IP
  • Load test or synthetic monitor exercising PATCH and GET flows in sequence
  • Shared corporate NAT where an editor's PATCH coincides with an anonymous visitor's GET
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the PATCH body for the correlated request and confirm it contains `__proto__`/`$pullAll`; confirm the paired GET returned record data with no bearer token. 2) Contain: block the source IP, revoke the editor token used on the PATCH, and restart the Node.js worker(s) to flush the polluted prototype. 3) Hunt: broaden the GET side to all piece-type endpoints and all source IPs (pollution is process-wide, so exploitation IP and abuse IP may differ); scope data accessed; confirm upgrade to 4.31.0.

let patches = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where CsMethod == "PATCH" and CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, CIp, PatchUri = CsUriStem;

| where CsMethod == "GET" and ScStatus == 200
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user", "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")

| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, GetTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), CIp, PatchUri, GetUri = CsUriStem
| order by GetTime desc

ApostropheCMS internet-exposed instance & vulnerable-surface inventory (CVE-2026-53609) AIReconnaissance High
Hunting inventory that surfaces every host serving the ApostropheCMS piece-type REST API (/api/v1/@apostrophecms/, /login/login) so the SOC can enumerate exposed, potentially-vulnerable (<= 4.30.0) instances and prioritise patching to 4.31.0. Not malicious on its own — an asset-exposure map to drive remediation. Rationale: Uses the article's unique URL surface (`/api/v1/@apostrophecms/`, `/@apostrophecms/login/login`) as an ApostropheCMS fingerprint. Access logs cannot read the running version, so pair the host list with a vuln scan / package audit to confirm <= 4.30.0. Corroborated version data: fixed in 4.31.0 (GitLab advisory / TheHackerWire). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/vulnerability/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • This is an inventory hunt — every legitimate ApostropheCMS site is expected to match; matches are not incidents
  • Non-Apostrophe apps that happen to proxy a path containing the string (rare)
  • Marketing/preview environments that are intentionally public
  • Already-patched 4.31.0+ instances still serving the same API surface
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each CsHost, resolve the owning team and check the deployed `apostrophe` npm version (package-lock, SBOM, or /health) against 4.31.0. 2) Contain: for any confirmed <= 4.30.0 internet-facing instance, prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0 and, if immediate patching is impossible, restrict editor accounts and put a WAF rule in front blocking PATCH bodies containing `__proto__`/`$pullAll`. 3) Hunt: on each confirmed-vulnerable host, retro-hunt the pollution-PATCH and auth-bypass UCs across the full log retention to rule out prior exploitation.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| summarize Requests = count(),
            DistinctSources = dcount(CIp),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SamplePaths = make_set(CsUriStem, 15),
            SawLogin = countif(CsUriStem has "/@apostrophecms/login/login")
          by CsHost
| order by Requests desc

Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where TargetFilePath endswith ".service" or TargetFilePath has "cron"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","rpm","dnf","crontab"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(systemctl|systemd|pacman|dpkg|apt|rpm|dnf|crontab)$/i

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Persistence-Path Binary Spawning SSH/SCP for Propagation (Atomic Arch Worm)
id: d7b3f981-2c44-4a90-9e15-3b8c6a1f2e57
description: Detects ssh/scp/sftp/rsync spawned by a parent process located in a malware persistence directory, matching the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH-worm self-propagation.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arch-linux-disables-aur-package-adoption-to-stop-malware-flood/

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/01
tags:

  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:

      - '/sftp'
      - '/rsync'
    ParentImage|contains:

level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(scp OR rsync OR sftp) @process.command_line:(*/var/lib/* OR */dev/shm/* OR */.config/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(ssh|scp|sftp|rsync)$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/(\/var\/lib\/|\/tmp\/|\/\.config\/|\/dev\/shm\/)/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(git|ansible|bash|sh|zsh|fish|rsync|ssh)$/i

ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")) (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*/var/lib/*","*/tmp/*","*/.config/*","*/dev/shm/*")) NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("git","ansible","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
