File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 18 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1204.004 T1218.005 T1218.011 T1528 T1539 T1547.001 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch fake 'browser/OS update' download from actor infrastructure · [LLM] ClickFix delivery: browser-spawned shell fetching CaptiveCrunch payload · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware deliver
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT dropper execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe · [LLM] CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' svchost32 persistence (service / Run key) · [LLM] Storm-2945 device-code phishing → Entra device registration via Auth Broker · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CaptiveCrunch C2 to Storm-2945 doppelganger M365 domains / infrastructure IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CaptiveCrunch C2 to Storm-2945 doppelganger M365 domains / infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint connections or DNS resolutions to the four Microsoft-mimicking phishing domains and six actor-controlled IPs used in the CaptiveCrunch AiTM/C2 infrastructure. Any traveler endpoint resolving ms365-device.com et al. or beaconing to these IPs is a direct IOC hit. Rationale: Uses the exact four doppelganger domains and six actor IPs from the article's KQL Block 2 and pre-extracted IOCs; ReliaQuest independently confirms the doppelganger-domain AiTM infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1557 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst detonating IOCs in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Proxy or SWG that pre-resolves/blocks the domain generating a telemetry hit without real user intent
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively probing the actor IPs
  • Recycled hosting IP reassigned to a benign tenant after takedown
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host and initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName). A browser hitting these = phishing; svchost32.exe/unsigned Go binary = confirmed CornFlake C2. Check whether the device was recently on hotel/conference Wi-Fi (public IP geo). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint in Defender/Falcon, block the four domains and six IPs at the proxy/firewall, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/refresh tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot on DeviceId for %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe execution and svchost32 service creation; check AADSignInEventsBeta for device-code auth to Microsoft Authentication Broker from the same user.
let target_domains = dynamic(["ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com"]);
let target_ips = dynamic(["31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any(target_domains) or RemoteIP in (target_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
let target_domains = dynamic(["ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com"]);
let target_ips = dynamic(["31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112"]);

(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where DnsQuery has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=DnsQuery, Kind="dns"),
(ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d) | where DstIpAddr in (target_ips) or Url has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SrcIpAddr, Host=SrcHostname, Indicator=strcat(DstIpAddr," ",Url), Kind="netsession")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake RAT dropper execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the CornFlake Go RAT after it copies itself into %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe during dropper mode. The svchost32 name in a user AppData path is a deliberate masquerade of the legitimate System32 svchost.exe and is unique to this campaign. Rationale: Anchors on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe from the article body and KQL Block 3; svchost32.exe in AppData (vs legit svchost.exe in System32) is a campaign-unique masquerade with near-zero legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Extremely rare — no legitimate Microsoft binary named svchost32.exe ships in a user AppData folder
  • A third-party app that coincidentally created a folder literally named svchost32 (essentially never observed)
  • Malware analyst intentionally executing a retrieved CornFlake sample on a monitored host
  • Security tool renaming/quarantining the sample preserving the original path in telemetry
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a browser or script interpreter parent confirms the ClickFix delivery chain; capture SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the svchost32 process tree, and delete the %APPDATA%\svchost32 folder; revoke the logged-on user's Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: search DeviceRegistryEvents for the svchost32 service / Run key, DeviceScheduledTaskEvents for named tasks, and DeviceNetworkEvents from this binary to the six actor IPs to map C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake 'Cloud Sync Service' svchost32 persistence (service / Run key) AIInstallation High
Detects CornFlake establishing persistence by registering a Windows service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider', or a Run key pointing at the svchost32 dropper. These exact strings are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service') and description ('Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider'), plus the Run-key/ImagePath pointing at the svchost32 dropper — all campaign-unique high-fidelity strings. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1547.001 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine third-party 'Cloud Sync' product using a similar description (verify the ImagePath — legit ones live in Program Files, not AppData)
  • Malware-analysis lab re-arming persistence for study on a monitored host
  • Backup/EDR agent registering an unrelated service that coincidentally contains the token 'sync'
  • GPO/config-management replaying a stale service definition (check InitiatingProcessFileName is not a management agent)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ServiceFileName/ImagePath resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (Program Files = likely benign; AppData = confirmed CornFlake). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the svchost32 service, Run key, and scheduled task, remove the AppData binary, and revoke user Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: enumerate all persistence surfaces (service, Run key, scheduled task, watchdog) since CornFlake uses redundant mechanisms; pivot on DeviceId for C2 to the six actor IPs.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32")
     or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe")
     or (RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
     or (RegistryValueData has "Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider")
     or (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValueData has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Storm-2945 device-code phishing → Entra device registration via Auth Broker AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Storm-2945/Storm-2372 device-code token-theft hallmark: a successful sign-in to the Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID (29d9ed98-...) targeting the Device Registration Service, enabling the actor to register a rogue device and mint a Primary Refresh Token. Catches the credential-access core of CaptiveCrunch's AiTM phishing. Rationale: The article ties CaptiveCrunch to Storm-2372's device-code/OAuth phishing leading to Entra device registration; the 2025 Storm-2372 Microsoft blog documents the exact Microsoft Authentication Broker client ID (29d9ed98-...) used to register a rogue device and obtain a PRT — the confirmed technical hallmark. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://thehackernews.com/2025/02/microsoft-russian-linked-hackers-using.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user enrolling a new personal/BYOD device via Microsoft Authenticator broker
  • Company-wide Intune/Entra device-registration rollout campaign
  • Help-desk assisted device onboarding for a traveling employee
  • MDM re-registration after an OS rebuild
Suppression filter
| where DeviceTrustType !in ("Hybrid Azure AD joined","Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the sign-in IPAddress/Location against the user's normal geo — hotel/airport/foreign IP during travel plus a brand-new device registration = high suspicion; inspect Entra Audit 'Add registered device' for the device name/owner. 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens and PRT, disable/quarantine the newly registered device object, and require re-MFA; consider a Conditional Access block on device-code flow. 3) Hunt: correlate this user with connections to the four doppelganger domains, and review Graph/M365 mailbox access from the new device identity for exfiltration.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker abused for device-code token theft
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ResourceDisplayName has "Device Registration"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, DeviceTrustType, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where AppId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e" or AppDisplayName =~ "Microsoft Authentication Broker"
| where ResultType == 0
| where ResourceDisplayName has "Device Registration"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent, IsInteractive, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch fake 'browser/OS update' download from actor infrastructure AIDelivery High
Detects executables, MSIs, or Android APKs written to disk whose download origin is one of the CaptiveCrunch actor domains or IPs — the fake browser/OS 'update' delivered via captive-portal redirection in response to browser connectivity checks. Ties the dropped file directly to Storm-2945 infrastructure. Rationale: Anchors the dropped fake-update file to the article's six actor IPs and four domains via FileOriginIP/FileOriginUrl; the article states malware masquerading as browser/OS updates (incl. APK for Android) is delivered from this infrastructure in response to connectivity checks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1189 T1557 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst downloading the sample from actor infra for analysis (Defender/Sentinel variants tie to actor IOC so this is the only realistic FP)
  • Datadog/Falcon variants (no IOC tie) may fire on legitimate software installers downloaded to Downloads/Temp via a browser
  • Auto-updaters (Chrome/Edge) staging updater .exe in user temp — exclude known updater signers
  • Portable-app users routinely downloading .exe to Downloads
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Google LLC","Microsoft Corporation","Mozilla Corporation")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm FileOriginIP/FileOriginUrl matches actor infra (Defender/Sentinel) — that's a definitive delivery hit; capture SHA256 and submit. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host if it was executed (check DeviceProcessEvents for svchost32), and block the origin IOC at the proxy. 3) Hunt: if executed, pivot to CornFlake persistence and C2 UCs; sweep other travelers on the same public IP/venue for the same download.

ClickFix delivery: browser-spawned shell fetching CaptiveCrunch payload AIDelivery High
Detects the ClickFix execution step where a script interpreter (PowerShell/cmd/mshta/curl) runs a command line referencing a CaptiveCrunch actor domain, IP, or the svchost32 drop path — the pasted 'fix' command victims run after the fake update/verification-failure prompt. Distinct from generic encoded-PowerShell rules by anchoring on actor IOCs. Rationale: Combines the article's ClickFix initial-access technique with the exact actor domains/IPs and svchost32 drop path — a script interpreter command line containing any of these strings is a high-fidelity ClickFix delivery signal that does not overlap generic encoded-PowerShell or Office-child-process rules. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/

  • Vulnerability scanner or connectivity test probing the actor domains via curl
  • Threat-intel automation curling the doppelganger domains for enrichment
  • SOAR playbook running validation against these IOCs

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and AccountName !in~ ("system","local service","network service")

1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine and parent (InitiatingProcessFileName) — a browser or explorer.exe parent confirms a ClickFix run-dialog paste; note any download URL/output path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the referenced domains/IPs, kill the process tree, and revoke the user's Entra sessions. 3) Hunt: check DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for the resulting %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and its service persistence; look for other users at the same venue running similar commands.

| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112","svchost32\\svchost32")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

NocoBase anonymous signup then immediate /api/myInAppChannels:list access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit) AIDelivery High
Correlates a successful POST /api/auth:signUp (enabled by default allowSignUp:true) with an access to the internal notification endpoint /api/myInAppChannels:list from the same source within seconds. A brand-new account touching that resource almost immediately is the exact CVE-2026-52887 access pattern; no legitimate user signs up and then hits the in-app-message channel list within seconds. Rationale: Uses the two article-named endpoints (/api/auth:signUp?authenticator=basic and /api/myInAppChannels:list) plus the documented allowSignUp:true default; the tight signup->channel-list temporal join is what separates exploitation from ordinary self-registration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated QA / synthetic-monitoring accounts that sign up and immediately exercise API endpoints
  • Load or penetration testing against a staging NocoBase instance
  • A shared NAT/proxy egress IP where an unrelated existing user hits the endpoint right after a new signup
  • Mobile app onboarding flow that pre-fetches notification channels post-registration
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP after signupTime; confirm the created username and whether the myInAppChannels:list request carried a filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] parameter (see SQLi UC). 2) Contain: disable/delete the newly-created account, and if exploitation is confirmed set allowSignUp:false on the auth-basic authenticator and block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: search the same IP/account for follow-on COPY ... TO PROGRAM payloads and for shell processes spawned by the postgres user in the DB container.
let Window = 5m;
let Signups = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/auth:signUp"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","201")
| project SignupTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/myInAppChannels:list"
| project ChannelsTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpStatusCode
| join kind=inner Signups on SrcIpAddr
| where ChannelsTime between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + Window)
| project SignupTime, ChannelsTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ChannelsTime, SignupTime), SrcIpAddr, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by SignupTime desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

CVE-2026-52887 SQL injection in NocoBase filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] parameter AIExploitation High
Flags HTTP requests to /api/myInAppChannels:list whose filter query carries the latestMsgReceiveTimestamp[$lt] operand with SQL syntax instead of a numeric epoch. The legitimate value is always an integer timestamp, so any SELECT / PG_SLEEP / UNION / COPY / TO PROGRAM / comment token in that field is a direct injection attempt. Rationale: The field name latestMsgReceiveTimestamp is unique to this vulnerable plugin, and the article's own payloads (PG_SLEEP(5), UNION SELECT, COPY...TO PROGRAM, -- comment) are exactly what must never appear in a numeric $lt operand, making this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (sqlmap/Burp) testing the endpoint from a known scanner IP
  • Internal red-team exercise against NocoBase
  • Security researchers validating the patch on a staging host
  • A WAF in monitor-only mode replaying archived attack traffic
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the full filter query string; a PG_SLEEP/CASE-WHEN value confirms a blind oracle, a COPY...TO PROGRAM value confirms attempted RCE. Note the authenticated account (Bearer token / username) and source IP. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, revoke/disable the offending NocoBase account, and upgrade @nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message to >=2.0.61. 3) Hunt: pivot to the DB container for postgres-spawned shells and TO PROGRAM statements, and check the users table for exfiltration of admin PBKDF2 hashes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("PG_SLEEP","pg_sleep","SELECT","UNION","COPY","PROGRAM","CASE WHEN","--",";")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PostgreSQL process spawning a shell inside NocoBase DB container (COPY TO PROGRAM RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the postgres backend process spawning /bin/sh, bash or dash — the observable side-effect of CVE-2026-52887's COPY ... TO PROGRAM stacked-statement RCE, which runs shell commands as uid=999(postgres) inside the database container. Postgres spawning an interactive/child shell is abnormal outside of rare archive/restore commands. Rationale: Maps directly to the article's verified RCE primitive (COPY ... TO PROGRAM running as uid=999(postgres)); a postgres->shell parent/child edge is the highest-fidelity host observable and is abnormal outside rare admin backup/restore hooks, which are excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p849-8hwh-84j9 • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/postgres/postgres_copy_from_program_cmd_exec/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate archive_command / restore_command hooks that pipe WAL through a shell
  • Backup tooling (barman, wal-g, pgBackRest) invoked by the postgres user
  • DBA running COPY ... TO PROGRAM for an approved ETL export
  • Container healthcheck scripts executed under the postgres UID
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("pg_basebackup","wal-e","wal-g","barman","pgbackrest","archive_command","restore_command")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell command line and any files it wrote (article shows /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt, /tmp/PWN_HASH.txt); correlate the timestamp back to a /api/myInAppChannels:list request in the web logs. 2) Contain: isolate/kill the DB container, rotate the NocoBase superuser and all DB credentials, and rebuild the postgres role without rolsuper. 3) Hunt: enumerate every shell child of postgres across all DB hosts, review the users table for exfiltrated PBKDF2 hashes, and check for outbound connections from the postgres process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "postgres"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pg_basebackup","wal-e","wal-g","barman","archive_command","restore_command"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "postgres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/ash","/zsh") or ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","zsh")
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pg_basebackup","wal-e","wal-g","barman","archive_command","restore_command"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

  • Security appliances/sandboxes detonating samples and generating the same C2 lookups
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS sinkhole services pre-resolving IOC domains
  • DNS logging proxies replaying historic queries during migration
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "digital.leroymerlin.com" and RemoteIP !in ("154.196.162.76","45.138.157.165","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) that resolved/connected to the IOC and whether the host is a Central Asian government/ministry asset in scope. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the domain+IP at the firewall/DNS, and capture memory (both families run in-memory with a minimal on-disk loader). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the loader on disk, secretsdump/fscan/pp.txt activity, an AnyDesk-named keylogger, and lateral net-use to admin shares; sweep the fleet for any other IOC-list domain or IP.

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX known sample hash execution or drop AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on process execution, image load, or file write matching the 16 MD5 hashes published for the OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX samples. Because both families are victim-specific and memory-resident, catching the minimal on-disk loader by hash is the cleanest execution-stage signal. Rationale: Directly uses the 16 published MD5s spanning OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX; hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity execution/install signal for memory-resident, victim-encoded loaders that otherwise leave minimal disk footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the samples in a monitored analysis VM
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies retaining the file and re-triggering file events
  • Threat-intel researchers storing IOC samples on a corporate share
  • Hash collision is effectively nil for MD5 at this scale but re-used loader stub across benign packers is theoretically possible
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\\Sandbox\\", @"\\Analysis\\", @"\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not an analysis sandbox) and record host, user, path and initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the sample, and capture volatile memory before reboot since the real payload lives in RAM. 3) Hunt: pull the loader's parent chain, look for the drive-serial/computer-name-keyed decode routine, and sweep for the C2 IOCs, secretsdump, fscan/pp.txt and AnyDesk-named keylogger across the estate.

Impacket secretsdump domain-controller hash extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts command-line invocation of Impacket's secretsdump against domain controllers, matching the campaign's post-compromise step of harvesting password hashes from DCs. Anchors on secretsdump / -just-dc flags rather than LSASS access, so it complements existing credential-theft rules. Rationale: Article states hashes were harvested from domain controllers using Impacket's secretsdump.py; the secretsdump string plus -just-dc* flags are the tool's canonical invocation and rarely legitimate in production. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises legitimately running Impacket
  • AD security assessments using secretsdump for auditing
  • A pentest tool named similarly living in a security team's toolkit share
  • Detection engineering validating this very rule with an atomic test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\RedTeam\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("PENTEST-01","SECAUDIT-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source host/user is an authorized pentest asset; check the target (DC hostname) and whether -just-dc dumped NTDS. 2) Contain: disable the executing account, isolate the host, and treat all domain credentials as potentially compromised — begin krbtgt double-reset planning. 3) Hunt: correlate with the campaign C2 IOCs, look for prior remote-interactive logons to the DC, Pandora RC remote access, and subsequent lateral net-use to admin shares.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger execution from non-standard path AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a process named like AnyDesk that is NOT the genuine signed AnyDesk binary, matching the campaign's keylogger that masquerades as AnyDesk to evade detection. Filters out the legitimate AnyDesk Software GmbH signed install. Rationale: Article states the keylogger 'masquerades as AnyDesk to sidestep detection'; matching an anydesk-named binary that lacks the AnyDesk Software GmbH signature and runs from a user-writable path isolates the impostor from genuine remote-support usage. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/unpacked AnyDesk run from Downloads by a legitimate support tech (usually still signed — the Company filter catches it)
  • Software-deployment staging AnyDesk to a ProgramData cache before install
  • Renamed legitimate AnyDesk copies by IT for allow-listing tests
  • Older AnyDesk builds with missing version metadata
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "AnyDesk"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the binary's signer/hash — a genuine AnyDesk is signed by 'AnyDesk Software GmbH'; an unsigned/mismatched one from a user path is the keylogger. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and force-reset credentials typed on that host (keystrokes are captured). 3) Hunt: look for the parent loader, browser-password decryption of Chrome/Firefox, secretsdump, and outbound C2 to the campaign domains from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "anydesk"
| where not (FolderPath has @"\AnyDesk\" and (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "AnyDesk" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "AnyDesk"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anydesk"
| where not (ActingProcessName has @"\AnyDesk\" and ActingProcessFileCompany has "AnyDesk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fscan internal/public port scan using 'pp.txt' credential file AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts execution of Fscan-style network scanning that references the campaign's 'pp.txt' password file and targets SSH (22) and MySQL (3306), matching the described lateral-discovery step. Anchors on the specific pp.txt filename plus fscan/port artefacts for high fidelity. Rationale: Article names Fscan scanning SSH/22 and MySQL/3306 and using credentials from a password file 'pp.txt'; the literal pp.txt string and fscan binary are distinctive and unlikely to appear in benign admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1046 T1110.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scans that happen to use fscan
  • A file literally named pp.txt used for unrelated benign purpose (rare in a cmdline arg)
  • Red-team engagement running fscan with a credential list
  • Network engineers troubleshooting SSH/MySQL reachability with a scripted scanner
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("VULNSCAN-01","PENTEST-01") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\Nessus\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the scanning host is not an authorized scanner; review the fscan target ranges and whether pp.txt credentials succeeded against 22/3306. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate any credentials present in pp.txt, and review SSH/MySQL auth logs on scanned hosts for successful access. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's C2 IOCs, secretsdump activity, and any resulting lateral net-use / Pandora RC remote sessions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "pp.txt"
    or FileName has "fscan"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "fscan"
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("-pwdf", "3306"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has "pp.txt" or CommandLine has "fscan" or NewProcessName endswith "\\fscan.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fscan Port Scan With pp.txt Credential File
id: b1e4d7c8-5a2f-4b90-8d63-1c9e0a4f2b76
description: Detects Fscan network scanning referencing the OctLurk/SilkLurk pp.txt password file

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/(pp\.txt|fscan)/i OR ImageFileName=/\\fscan\.exe$/i)

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*pp.txt*" OR Processes.process_name="fscan.exe" OR Processes.process="*fscan*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search (process="*pp.txt*" OR process="*fscan*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
SilkLurk collection: admin-share doc staging archived with WinRAR/7-Zip AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts WinRAR/7-Zip archiving spawned from cmd/PowerShell that follows connecting to network shares with admin credentials, matching SilkLurk's document-theft workflow (net use to admin shares → stage confidential docs → archive with WinRAR/7-Zip). Pairs the archiver child with a shell parent for fidelity. Rationale: Article describes SilkLurk using cmd→PowerShell to reach admin shares, stage confidential docs and archive them specifically with WinRAR and 7-Zip; the shell-parent + archiver-child + create/password flags combination isolates staging from interactive user archiving. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin backup scripts archiving directories with 7-Zip/WinRAR from a scheduled cmd/PowerShell task
  • Software packaging or log-bundling jobs creating password-protected archives
  • Helpdesk collecting diagnostic bundles via a PowerShell wrapper
  • Developers scripting release-artifact zips with rar.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Backup", "backup", "\\Scripts\\") and AccountName in~ ("svc-backup","backupadmin"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the archive command (source paths, output name, -hp password) and whether the parent shell recently ran net use to a C$/ADMIN$ share. 2) Contain: isolate the host, locate and preserve the archive before exfil, and block outbound to the campaign C2 IOCs. 3) Hunt: check for the preceding admin-share net use, SilkLurk DLL side-load/PlugX on the host, and any outbound transfer of the archive to non-corporate IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" a ", "-hp", " -p", "-r ", "a -r")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\rar.exe", "\\winrar.exe", "\\7z.exe", "\\7za.exe", "\\7zg.exe")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe", "\\powershell.exe", "\\pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (" a ", "-hp", " -p", "-r ", "a -r")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRAR/7-Zip Data Staging Spawned By Shell (SilkLurk)
id: e7c2a9d5-4f38-4b1c-90a7-6d2e8b0f3c41
description: Detects WinRAR/7-Zip archive creation launched by cmd/PowerShell consistent with SilkLurk document staging
references:
  - https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/01
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1560.001
  - attack.t1039
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\7z.exe'
      - '\7za.exe'
      - '\7zg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ' a '
      - '-hp'
      - ' -p'
      - '-r '
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\PowerShell.exe) @Image:(*\rar.exe OR *\winrar.exe OR *\7z.exe OR *\7za.exe OR *\7zg.exe OR *\WinRAR.exe OR *\Rar.exe) @CommandLine:(*" a "* OR *-hp* OR *" -p"* OR *"-r "*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/\\(rar|winrar|7z|7za|7zg)\.exe$/i
| regex("(\\sa\\s|-hp|\\s-p|-r\\s)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="* a *" OR Processes.process="*-hp*" OR Processes.process="* -p*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("rar.exe","winrar.exe","7z.exe","7za.exe","7zg.exe") AND Processes.parent_process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND (Processes.process="* a *" OR Processes.process="*-hp*" OR Processes.process="* -p*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"

SecurityEvent

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.credential-access

    product: windows

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'

falsepositives:
